why.headline: Strong hips push you off the ground for dives and jumps.

claims.text: Your hips drive the push into a dive. In elite adult keepers, weaker-side dives had less hip push at take-off.
Saves are short, explosive dives and jumps. In a youth trial, hip and trunk drills raised jump height.
Early-teen players added five moves, including a back bridge, 4 times weekly. After 26 weeks, jumps were 5 to 6.8% higher.
Older teen players added a weighted hip lift once a week. After 20 weeks, sprints were 3 to 3.8% faster.

keep_up.text: Keep training it every week to keep gains coming. In one youth study, jump gains lasted 8 weeks after training stopped. Everyone improves at their own pace.

map.plain: The muscles at the back of your thighs

note.text: Bridge studies measured these muscles in adults; none measured them in teens.

claims.text: The bridge works your hips while the floor holds your back. In studies with adults, these muscles worked at under half effort.
Studies in young people find strength rises far more than muscle size. Early gains are mostly your nerves learning to switch muscles on.

limits.text: No study has tested the bridge alone in goalkeepers. The youth trials used several exercises, one with a barbell.
